name: Ostrogothic Kingdom

imageInfo.caption: A modern map of Theodoric's power at its height in 523, with the Ostrogothic kingdom itself in dark red and the kingdoms he dominated through marriage and arms in pink.
imageInfo.creator: SelfieCity (Wikimedia Commons), after Howard Wiseman
imageInfo.note: A modern reconstruction rather than a surviving ancient map, redrawn from Howard Wiseman's Empire of Theodoric the Great 523 over a blank base map. It carries no place names and no legend, only a scale bar in kilometres and miles, so the two shades have to be read from the caption: dark red is the kingdom Theodoric ruled directly — Italy, Sicily, Dalmatia, Provence and the Alpine provinces, including the strip of Burgundy between the Durance and the Isère annexed in 523 — while pink marks the realms under his hegemony rather than his rule. Hispania is shown dark because Theodoric governed the Visigothic kingdom as regent for his grandson Amalaric from 511, which is a stronger claim than the map's single colour implies. 523 is the year before the arrests of Boethius and Symmachus, so the map shows the kingdom immediately before the crisis the article describes. Licensed CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary: The Ostrogothic Kingdom ruled Italy from 493 to 553, preserving Roman administration under Gothic kings until Justinian's armies destroyed it.
overview: Under Theodoric it was the most successful of the barbarian successor states. Sixty years later it had been fought out of existence, and Italy with it.
knownFor: Theodoric the Great ruled Italy for thirty-three years keeping Roman law and administration intact.
Ravenna as its capital, where its churches and mosaics survive.
Arian kings ruling a Catholic population, without systematic persecution.
Destroyed in the Gothic War of 535–554, which ruined Italy in the process.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The Ostrogothic Kingdom held Italy from 493 until 553, founded by Theodoric the Great after he killed Odoacer and took Ravenna.
It was in many ways the most successful of the successor states. Roman law, the Senate, the civil administration and the consulship all continued, with a Gothic army and a Gothic king above them.
It ended in nineteen years of war with Justinian's empire, which reconquered Italy and in doing so destroyed the thing worth reconquering.

contentSections.title: Theodoric and the settlement
paragraphs: Theodoric entered Italy in 489 on the eastern emperor's commission, defeated Odoacer over four years, and killed him personally at a banquet in 493.

What followed was a deliberate division of labour. The Goths were the army and held land assignments; the Romans ran the administration, the courts and the cities, and Roman law continued to apply to them.
Theodoric ruled thirty-three years from Ravenna, corresponded with Constantinople as a legitimate authority, and left the buildings and mosaics that are the kingdom's most visible survival.

contentSections.title: Religion and the Roman elite
paragraphs: The Goths were Arian Christians and the Italian population Catholic, and for most of Theodoric's reign that difference was managed rather than fought over.

It soured at the end. Suspicion of Roman senatorial contacts with Constantinople led to the execution of Boethius around 524 — a philosopher whose Consolation of Philosophy, written in prison awaiting death, became one of the most read books of the Middle Ages.
That episode did lasting damage to the kingdom's standing with the Roman elite whose cooperation it depended on.

contentSections.title: The succession crisis
paragraphs: Theodoric died in 526 leaving a ten-year-old grandson, Athalaric, with his daughter Amalasuintha as regent — an educated, Romanised woman who governed capably and was resented for it.
Athalaric died in 534. Amalasuintha took her cousin Theodahad as co-ruler and he had her imprisoned and murdered in 535.
Justinian had been in correspondence with Amalasuintha and used her murder as his justification for war. Whether he wanted the pretext or merely accepted it is a question the sources cannot settle.

contentSections.title: Major rulers
paragraphs: Theodoric the Great (493–526) is the kingdom in every meaningful sense: he made it, defined its settlement with the Roman population, and left it at its height.
Athalaric (526–534) reigned as a child under Amalasuintha's regency; Theodahad (534–536) murdered her, lost Sicily and Naples, and was killed by his own side for incompetence.

Vitiges (536–540) besieged Belisarius in Rome for a year and eventually surrendered at Ravenna. After a brief interval, Totila (541–552) recovered most of Italy before being killed at Taginae, and Teias (552–553) was the last king.

contentSections.title: Government, society and economy
paragraphs: The kingdom ran on inherited Roman machinery: the praetorian prefecture, the tax system, the city councils and the courts continued much as before.
Cassiodorus, who served as Theodoric's minister, left a collection of official letters that is the single best window into how the administration actually worked.
The Goths were a minority — an army and a landholding class rather than a settling population — and the distance between them and the Romans, in law, religion and language, was never closed.

contentSections.title: The Gothic War and the end
paragraphs: Justinian's forces took Sicily in 535 and Belisarius entered Rome in 536 and Ravenna in 540, and the kingdom looked finished.
It was not. Totila recovered nearly all of Italy in the 540s, and the war ran on until Narses destroyed the Gothic army at Taginae in 552 and Teias at Mons Lactarius the following year.

The surviving Goths were permitted to leave Italy on terms. The kingdom simply ended, and the Italy that remained was so exhausted that the Lombards took much of it in 568 with comparatively little difficulty.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: Its lasting monuments are in Ravenna — the mausoleum of Theodoric, the churches and the mosaics — and in the books that came out of it, above all Boethius and Cassiodorus.
Its political lesson is bleaker. The most successful attempt to run a post-Roman state on Roman lines was destroyed not by barbarian rivals but by the Roman empire itself.
The reconquest that ended it is the clearest case in this archive of a war that achieved its objective and lost the thing it was fought for.

timeline.title: Theodoric enters Italy
timeline.description: Theodoric crosses into Italy on the eastern emperor's commission to remove Odoacer.

timeline.title: Kingdom founded
timeline.description: Theodoric kills Odoacer at Ravenna and takes Italy.

timeline.title: Execution of Boethius
timeline.description: The philosopher is executed on suspicion of treasonable contact with Constantinople.

timeline.title: Death of Theodoric
timeline.description: Theodoric dies leaving a child heir and a regency.

timeline.title: Athalaric dies
timeline.description: The boy king dies; Amalasuintha takes Theodahad as co-ruler.

timeline.title: Murder of Amalasuintha
timeline.description: Theodahad has her killed, giving Justinian his justification for war.

timeline.title: Belisarius takes Rome
timeline.description: Byzantine forces enter Rome; the Gothic position in the south collapses.

timeline.title: The siege of Rome
timeline.description: Vitiges besieges Belisarius in Rome for a year and nine days and fails.

timeline.title: Ravenna falls
timeline.description: Vitiges surrenders the capital; the kingdom appears finished.

timeline.title: Totila's recovery
timeline.description: Totila retakes most of Italy, including Rome twice, and offers peace repeatedly.

timeline.title: Taginae
timeline.description: Narses destroys the Gothic army and Totila is killed.

timeline.title: The kingdom ends
timeline.description: Teias is killed at Mons Lactarius and the surviving Goths leave Italy on terms.

armsImageInfo.caption: The Ostrogothic kingdom bore no coat of arms; Theodoric's device was his monogram, carved in the roundel at the top of this capital of his reign in the Piazza del Popolo at Ravenna.
armsImageInfo.creator: Ostrogothic stonecarver at Ravenna; photographed by the Commons contributor Sailko
armsImageInfo.date: the capital of Theodoric’s reign, 493 to 526; photographed 2013
armsImageInfo.note: Heraldry did not exist in the sixth century, so the Ostrogothic kingdom had no arms and no flag; the monogram was the closest thing to a personal device Theodoric used, and it appears on his buildings, his bricks and his chancery documents. The capital stands in the loggia of the Venetian palace on the Piazza del Popolo in Ravenna, and the column beneath it is thought to have been taken from one of the Arian churches Theodoric built and the Venetians later pulled down, so the capital is in its second home rather than its first. The monogram itself is the small carved roundel at the top centre of the frame, not the whole capital, and the acanthus below it is ordinary late Roman work. Licensed CC BY-SA 3.0.
